b: Francis Lawrence revisits the world of The Hunger Games for a bruising prequel that gives one of the franchise’s most beloved characters the origin story he deserves.

For those of us who grew up with The Hunger Games, the chance to return to this world and discover the story behind one of its most beloved characters has been a long time coming. Francis Lawrence’s latest instalment, Sunrise on the Reaping, is a gripping, emotionally bruising prequel that justifies the anticipation and proves that the franchise still has plenty to say.

Set 24 years before Katniss Everdeen volunteers as tribute, the film begins on the morning of the 50th Hunger Games, a Second Quarter Quell in which twice the usual number of children are sent to their deaths. It also happens to be the sixteenth birthday of Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada), a bright-eyed young man living in District 12 with his mother and younger brother Sid (Smylie Bradwell). Haymitch and his girlfriend Lenore Dove (Whitney Peak) while away their days in the meadow, tending geese and dreaming of a life beyond the Capitol. That is, until he is forced to fight for his own survival in the 50th Hunger Games.

Zada has some sizeable boots to fill, stepping into a role made so memorably sardonic in the original trilogy by Woody Harrelson. And yet he is an absolute standout, capturing the character’s soft drawl and infectious charm while bringing a tenderness of his own to this younger version. Zada’s Haymitch is something of a mother hen, his youthful bravado tempered by a vulnerability that makes his fate all the more affecting. He’s in good company, too, with Mckenna Grace and Ben Wang among an impressive crop of younger talent joining him as fellow tributes.

The film also boasts an impressive line-up of industry giants, whose inspired casting makes their younger incarnations instantly recognisable. Jesse Plemons is a canny choice for Plutarch Heavensbee, while Elle Fanning nails Effie Trinket’s blend of flamboyance and warmth. Ralph Fiennes is unsurprisingly excellent as President Snow, his quiet menace every bit as sinister as the late Donald Sutherland’s iteration. With its familiar faces and knowing nods to the original films, this one is particularly rewarding viewing for longtime fans.

One of the film’s greatest strengths, however, lies in its striking visual design. The arena is a technicolour poison paradise, with lush landscapes and an unnaturally vibrant palette lifted straight from author Suzanne Collins’ page. It’s a world that feels both familiar and newly realised, while the increasingly elaborate Games deliver the spectacle you’d hope for from a big-screen outing.

As the tragedies mount and the pieces fall into place, it becomes painfully clear how Haymitch grows into the hardened mentor we meet decades later. There’s a cruel irony to watching his hopes unravel, offset by the knowledge that his time will eventually come, though not before he has endured so much more. It’s a devastating addition to the story.

Unlike the comparatively muted The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes from 2023, Sunrise on the Reaping makes a proper return to the original films’ winning formula. It’s a reminder of just how compelling this world can be when its exhilarating spectacle and deeply human storytelling are firing on all cylinders. With Zada at its centre, Haymitch’s story proves well worth the wait.
